justification: Re-fetching the two primary comparison pages confirms round 5's read of the field. MS Learn's array reference (2,594 words) is a syntax catalogue: single/multi-dimensional/jagged declaration forms, indexing, foreach order, implicitly typed arrays -- no memory-layout diagram, no cache/locality content, no List<T> internals, no measurements of any kind. Wikipedia's Dynamic Array article has real conceptual depth (geometric-expansion diagram, a 12-language growth-factor comparison table, an amortized-cost explanation) but stays at pseudocode: no runnable code, no C#-specific detail beyond naming List<T> in passing, no benchmarks. Neither page comes close to this article's four hand-drawn, theme-correct diagrams; its 35 runnable code blocks building a real measured argument (row- vs column-major traversal, TLB/cache-line reuse distance with a targeted band-tiling experiment, List<T> internals read from the actual dotnet/runtime source, exact Insert/RemoveAt element-move counts, a reproduced CollectionsMarshal.AsSpan-over-List<T> use-after-grow hazard); or its six exercises with real worked solutions. That alone places it in the 'clearly better than the best existing result' tier the 10-anchor describes. What holds it at 9.0 rather than higher: the round-5 blocker and major are both now genuinely resolved -- Lighthouse performance measured 99, 100, 100 across three serial runs this round (accessibility/best-practices/SEO 100/100/100 on every run, zero console errors, zero broken links), and the main document's network record this round shows transferSize 32,040 bytes against resourceSize 390,508 bytes (about 8.2%), confirming real compression is now applied rather than the intermittent failure round 5 caught; the four figure captions read 1 (int[] memory layout, part04), 2 (cache-line reuse distance, part08), 3 (Insert/RemoveAt shift, part16), 4 (rectangular vs jagged grids, part21-22) in that order both in the source and on screen, in both themes, with every label legible at 390px and no faded/scrolling edge on any of the four. But two round-5 minors were in scope for the writer and were not touched in this exception round: the five-column 'Same sum, two loop orders' table still crowds its rightmost (evidence) column against the phone edge, and the same handful of code lines (the grid[2,3] WriteLine in the offsets block; the List<int> as span / LinkedList<int> Report(...) calls and their SumSpan/SumLinked signatures in the containers block) still clip their tails on a 390px screen. Both are genuine, if minor, unresolved nits against WRITER_GUIDE section 7, which is why this stays at 9.0 and not a clean 10.
